explanation: Fires on the verb or particle that expresses someone or something arriving at or becoming part of a group or place: 'join(ed)/rejoin' (joined the club/society), 'came to/over to' (came to the U.S.), 'stopped by', 'show up'. It fires on the movement/joining word itself, or on the 'to' right after 'come'. Weaker on other words in 'come to'/'bring to' phrases ('back', 'the', 'boarded'), and near zero on ordinary infinitive 'to'.

Fires on CSS class-name or selector tokens in HTML class attributes, CSS rules and jQuery selectors, usually the second or later part of a hyphenated or space-separated class list (weui-cell 'ui', 'table-header', 'col-md', 'form-control', '.tab', 'pull-right'). Strongest in a multi-class string inside class="...". Near zero outside front-end markup.

Fires inside the names of synthetic chemicals, pesticides, drugs and pollutants (DDT/DDE, polychlorinated, isoxazoles, CFCs, trichlorfon, polyisoprene), and on the function words that introduce them in toxicology or chemistry text ('use of', 'resistance to azoles and', 'agents like'). Strongest in pesticide or pollutant contexts. Weak on general text.

Fires on the first word of a technical compound noun in computing text, chiefly 'System', 'data', 'time' and 'input' as modifiers ('System.Media', 'system stored procs', 'data table', 'data packet', 'time series', 'input_index', 'System Administrator'). It also fires on similar words like State, Current and Get. Mid-range on other noun modifiers such as 'service advisors' and 'field'. Weak elsewhere.

A mixture. Its strongest hits are 'appeal' in 'This appeal involves/concerns' in court opinions. It also fires on the digit after the journal code in '{#sec1-journal-17-0...' section anchors, Java package/import tokens, '<head' in HTML, and headline phrases ('good news', 'Need to Know'), plus assorted unrelated words. Beyond the legal 'this appeal' case it is hard to predict.

Fires on the middle piece of a fixed multi-token technical term, where the next piece is almost certain: 'factors of' in 'prime factors of', 'spect' in 'mass spectrometry', 'composite' number, 'il' in bronchodilator, 'ac' in visual acuity, 'AM' in PER CURIAM, 'receiver operating'. Fires most strongly in math-problem and analytical-chemistry text. Weak on ordinary words.

Fires on the first token after a script or language switch, such as katakana word starts in Japanese text, Devanagari, Chinese inside English, or 'Okay'. It also fires on sentence- and clause-initial words in English prose ('The', 'However', 'Their', 'same', 'such'). No single feature explains all of these. Hard to predict.

Fires on words about genetics, breeding and reproduction: crossed/cross, mating, offspring, diploids, mutations, recombination, germ line, reproduction, progenitor, clonal, evolution, genetic diversity, parents/progeny. It fires on the concept word itself, most strongly in plant or animal breeding and genetics text. Weak on unrelated biology.

Fires on the separator inside namespaced or compound identifiers: the ':' in XML namespace prefixes (xmlns:android, xsi:schemaLocation, f:metadata, telerik:), the '-' inside citation keys ([@b16-27], #sec1-ijerph, @B7-sensors), and BEM '__'. Weaker on hyphens in chemical names and party abbreviations (PML-F). The separator token is what matters.

Mostly fires on words in political, military and sports-contest news: vote/voted, fighting, defeat, against, the first names or 'al' particles of political figures (Vladimir Putin, Omar al Razzaz), party abbreviations (SPD), and set scores (3-2, 6-5). The top hit, the '.' in a jQuery version URL, does not fit this. Moderate on violence or crime news words.

Fires very strongly on the 'A' that starts 'A:' answer headers in Q&A (StackExchange-style) text, right after a question block. It also fires on similar label tokens before a colon ('public:' in C++), and on 'per' as a word start in French/Portuguese ('perçus', 'perseg') or 'per cent'. A standalone 'A' after a question is the clear main trigger.

Fires on an opening quotation mark (", ', “, «), especially one that opens a string literal in code (SQL, JavaScript, Python) or a direct quotation in prose after 'said:', 'says', 'like,'. The token itself (an opening quote, often with a leading space) is what matters. Closing quotes and other punctuation are weak.

Fires on 'for' in the counsel lines of court opinions ('Name, City, for appellant/plaintiff/respondent'), and on the period/newline that ends such an attorney listing. Outside legal headers it gives only scattered weak or moderate hits (e.g. 'Hind III', 'Share this').

Mixed. It fires on '.com' in CDN URLs (bootstrapcdn.com), on a few C++ header names, on vivid evaluative adjectives (hilarious, astonishing, inexpensive, bewildered), and heavily on tokens inside non-Latin scripts (Japanese katakana, Devanagari conjuncts, Chinese, Vietnamese). There is no common thread.
